metadata.file_name: English digital reading achievement for East Asian students  identifying the key predictors using a machine learning approach.pdf
metadata.title: English digital reading achievement for East Asian students: identifying the key predictors using a machine learning approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 microdata for 15-year-olds from Macao, Hong Kong, and Singapore who completed the English version of the digital reading assessment. The manuscript does not report whether PISA sampling/student weights or replicate weights were applied in the random-forest regression, nor does it name any weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife). Because the analysis is implemented with the R randomForest package, the authors appear to have conducted an unweighted ML analysis, which is common when ML algorithms are used without native complex-survey weight support. For replication with population-representative inference, analysts should apply PISA complex-sample weights and, if available, replicate weights when estimating uncertainty, while also ensuring that any preprocessing (including missing-data handling) is performed within resampling folds to avoid leakage.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Participants were selected from PISA 2018 after ensuring availability of digital reading performance and the 24 independent variables (including ICT literacy/attitudes, self-efficacy, growth mindset, SES, language exposure, and disciplinary climate). The analytic sample was restricted to students in Macao, Hong Kong, and Singapore who wrote the English version of the test. The paper also indicates that students without English test language or without data on the variables used in the study could not be included, implying listwise exclusion for missingness on key predictors/outcome after the stated missing-data preprocessing.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Digital Reading (English test language), ages 15 (15-year-olds), Macao/Hong Kong/Singapore
main_findings.target_variable: English digital reading achievement (predicted by random forest regression)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Random forest regression with 24 predictors; ten-fold cross-validation with five repeats. Mean decreased MSE: Top 1 = 13799.62, Top 3 = 8453.425, Top 6 = 6527.657, Top 12 = 5239.434, Top 24 = 4766.158. Top 12 predictors explained 70.3% of the variance; mean squared residuals at Top 12 = 4664.21.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Digital Reading (English test language) data for 15-year-olds from Macao, Hong Kong, and Singapore, the study leveraged socioeconomic status (SES), ICT use during lessons, interest in ICT, home language, and language exposure from best friends to predict English digital reading achievement, finding that SES and ICT-related factors were the most influential predictors and that the top 12 variables explained 70.3% of the variance. This indicates that strengthening equitable access to ICT-rich learning opportunities and supporting students’ ICT interest/engagement—alongside addressing SES-linked resource gaps—may be a high-leverage strategy for improving digital reading outcomes, though the study’s predictive ML design and limited reporting on survey-weight/PV handling mean causal claims cannot be inferred.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 digital reading achievement in English for 7,703 15-year-olds from Macao (N=679), Hong Kong (N=348), and Singapore (N=6,676), restricting to students who took the English version of the test and had the required variables. Using a random-forest regression model with 24 predictors drawn from individual, microsystem, and mesosystem levels, the authors rank variable importance via mean decrease in accuracy (MDA) and select a robust subset using ten-fold cross-validation with five repeats. Prediction error (mean decreased MSE) decreases as predictors are added, with the top 12 variables achieving a mean decreased MSE of 5239.434 and explaining 70.3% of the variance (mean squared residuals at 4664.21). The most consistently important factors include SES, ICT-related variables (especially subject-related ICT use during lessons and interest in ICT), and language exposure measures. Limitations include the absence of explicit complex-survey weight reporting, inferred PV handling, and the fact that the analysis is cross-sectional and predictive rather than causal.
